topic.name: Second-Degree Taylor Polynomials of Multivariable Functions

question.text: For the function of two variables $ f\left(x,y \right) = e^{x-2y}, $ the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0, 0)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) = 1 + x + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a}\,y + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b} xy + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{c} y^2. \] Find the value of $a+b+c.$
question.explanation:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

\begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx \overbrace{f(0,0) + f_x(0,0) \cdot x + f_y(0,0) \cdot y}^{\large \textrm{Linear approximation}} \\[5pt] &\phantom{\approx}\:\: + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2} \left( f_{xx}(0,0) \cdot x^2 + 2 f_{xy}(0,0) \cdot xy + f_{yy}(0,0) \cdot y^2 \right)}_{\large \textrm{Quadratic part}}. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have \begin{align*} f(0,0) &= 1. \end{align*}

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_x(x,y) &= e^{x-2y}, &\quad f_y(x,y) &= -2e^{x-2y} \\[5pt] f_x(0,0) &= 1, &\quad f_y(0,0) &= -2 \end{align*}

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_{xx}(x,y) & = e^{x-2y}, & \quad f_{xx}(0,0) &= 1\\[5pt] f_{xy}(x,y) &= -2e^{x-2y}, & \quad f_{xy}(0,0) &= -2 \\[5pt] f_{yy}(x,y) & = 4e^{x-2y} , & \quad f_{yy}(0,0) & = 4 \end{align*}

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

\begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx 1 + 1 \cdot x + (-2) \cdot y + \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 1 \cdot x^2 + 2 (-2) \cdot xy + 4 \cdot y^2 \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 + x + (\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-2})y + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + (\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-2})xy + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}y^2. \end{align*}

Finally,

\[ a+b+c = (-2) + (-2) + 2 = -2. \]

question.text: For the function of two variables $ f(x,y) = e^{xy}, $ the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0, 0)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a} + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}xy. \] Find the value of $a+b.$
question.explanation:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx \overbrace{f(0,0) + f_x(0,0) \cdot x + f_y(0,0) \cdot y}^{\large \textrm{Linear approximation}} \\[5pt] & \phantom{\approx}\:\: + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2} \left( f_{xx}(0,0) \cdot x^2 + 2 f_{xy}(0,0) \cdot xy + f_{yy}(0,0) \cdot y^2 \right)}_{\large \textrm{Quadratic part}}. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have \begin{align*} f(0,0) & = 1. \end{align*}

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = ye^{xy}, &\quad f_y(x,y) &= xe^{xy} \\[5pt] f_x(0,0) & = 0, & \quad f_y(0,0) & = 0 \end{align*}

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_{xx}(x,y) & = y^2 e^{xy}, & \quad f_{xx}(0,0) &= 0\\[5pt] f_{xy}(x,y) &= (1+xy)e^{xy}, & \quad f_{xy}(0,0) &= 1 \\[5pt] f_{yy}(x,y) & = x^2e^{xy} , & \quad f_{yy}(0,0) & = 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx 1 + 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 0 \cdot x^2 + 2 (1) \cdot xy + 0 \cdot y^2 \right) \\[5pt] & = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1} + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}xy. \end{align*}

Finally, \[ a + b = 1 + 1 = 2. \]

question.text: For the function of two variables $ f(x,y) = e^{x^2 + y^2}, $ the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a} + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{c}y^2. \] Find the value of $a + b + c.$
question.explanation:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx \overbrace{f(0,0) + f_x(0,0) \cdot x + f_y(0,0) \cdot y}^{\large \textrm{Linear approximation}} \\[5pt] & \phantom{\approx}\:\: + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2} \left( f_{xx}(0,0) \cdot x^2 + 2 f_{xy}(0,0) \cdot xy + f_{yy}(0,0) \cdot y^2 \right)}_{\large \textrm{Quadratic part}}. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have \begin{align*} f(0,0) & = 1. \end{align*}

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = 2xe^{x^2+y^2}, & \quad f_y(x,y) &= 2ye^{x^2+y^2} \\[5pt] f_x(0,0) & = 0, & \quad f_y(0,0) & = 0 \end{align*}

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_{xx}(x,y) & = 2(1+2x^2)e^{x^2+y^2}, & \quad f_{xx}(0,0) &= 2\\[5pt] f_{xy}(x,y) &= 4xye^{x^2+y^2}, & \quad f_{xy}(0,0) &= 0 \\[5pt] f_{yy}(x,y) & = 2(1+2y^2)e^{x^2+y^2} , & \quad f_{yy}(0,0) & = 2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx 1 + 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 2 \cdot x^2 + 2 (0) \cdot xy + 2 \cdot y^2 \right) \\[5pt] & = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1} + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}y^2. \end{align*}

Finally, \[ a + b + c = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. \]

question.text: For the function of two variables $ f(x,y) = y\sin(x+y), $ the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a}xy + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}y^2. \] Find the value of $a + b.$
question.explanation:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx \overbrace{f(0,0) + f_x(0,0) \cdot x + f_y(0,0) \cdot y}^{\large \textrm{Linear approximation}} \\[5pt] & \phantom{\approx}\:\: + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2} \left( f_{xx}(0,0) \cdot x^2 + 2 f_{xy}(0,0) \cdot xy + f_{yy}(0,0) \cdot y^2 \right)}_{\large \textrm{Quadratic part}}. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have \begin{align*} f(0,0) & = 0. \end{align*}

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = y\cos(x+y), & \quad f_y(x,y) &= \sin(x+y)+y\cos(x+y) \\[5pt] f_x(0,0) & = 0, & \quad f_y(0,0) & = 0 \end{align*}

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_{xx}(x,y) & = -y\sin(x+y), & \quad f_{xx}(0,0) &= 0\\[5pt] f_{xy}(x,y) &= \cos(x+y)-y\sin(x+y), & \quad f_{xy}(0,0) &= 1 \\[5pt] f_{yy}(x,y) & = 2\cos(x+y)-y\sin(x+y) , & \quad f_{yy}(0,0) & = 2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx 0 + 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 0 \cdot x^2 + 2 (1) \cdot xy + 2 \cdot y^2 \right) \\[5pt] & = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}xy + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}y^2. \end{align*}

Finally, \[ a + b + c = 1 + 1 = 2. \]

question.text: For the function of two variables $ f(x,y) = \cos(x-2y), $ the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) = 1 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a}x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}xy + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{c}y^2. \] Find the value of $a + b + c.$
question.explanation:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx \overbrace{f(0,0) + f_x(0,0) \cdot x + f_y(0,0) \cdot y}^{\large \textrm{Linear approximation}} \\[5pt] & \phantom{\approx}\:\: + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2} \left( f_{xx}(0,0) \cdot x^2 + 2 f_{xy}(0,0) \cdot xy + f_{yy}(0,0) \cdot y^2 \right)}_{\large \textrm{Quadratic part}}. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have \begin{align*} f(0,0) & = 1. \end{align*}

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = -\sin(x-2y), & \quad f_y(x,y) &= 2\sin(x-2y) \\[5pt] f_x(0,0) & = 0, & \quad f_y(0,0) & = 0 \end{align*}

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: \begin{align*} f_{xx}(x,y) & = -\cos(x-2y), & \quad f_{xx}(0,0) &= -1\\[5pt] f_{xy}(x,y) &= 2\cos(x-2y), & \quad f_{xy}(0,0) &= 2 \\[5pt] f_{yy}(x,y) & = -4\cos(x-2y) , & \quad f_{yy}(0,0) & = -4 \end{align*}

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by \begin{align*} f(x,y) & \approx 1 + 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + \dfrac{1}{2} \left( -1 \cdot x^2 + 2 \left(2\right) \cdot xy + (-4) \cdot y^2 \right) \\[5pt] & = 1 + \left(\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-\dfrac{1}{2}}\right)x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}xy+ (\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-2})y^2. \end{align*}

Finally, \[ a + b + c = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2 + (-2) = - \dfrac{1}{2}. \]
